output.summary: Loyalty mobile app (points, rewards, push offers) for a 22-shop bakery chain replacing a paper stamp card, with old tills that have no API and unreliable internet in some shops. The closest past project is a coffee chain loyalty app (35 stores, same constraints), delivered in 760 hours / $70,000 after an estimate of 600. The main risks are the till integration, offline handling and the fixed anniversary deadline. This brief has fewer stores, so the range is adjusted slightly downward at the low end, but the hidden-cost lessons from the past project are kept.
open_questions: What is the anniversary campaign date, and is it a hard launch date or a target?
What till models and operating systems are in use, and is there a store computer attached to each till that could host an agent?
Can points be earned by scanning a customer QR code at the till, or is there another way to identify the customer and the purchase amount?
Which shops have unreliable internet, and is a delayed points sync (minutes to hours) acceptable to the business?
Is a back office needed for marketing to create campaigns and view redemptions?
How many customers are expected in the first six months, and do you need to import existing stamp card holders?
Do you need both iOS and Android, and is a cross-platform approach acceptable?
What is the points and rewards logic (per purchase, per amount, expiry, tiers)?
Who will support store staff, and what is their level of technical training?
Is there a budget ceiling for the first version?

risks.description: Software must be installed on old store machines to send points because the tills have no API. Differing Windows versions and flaky internet made this the main source of overrun on the comparable project, and it needs its own estimate line.

citations.quote: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate.
The registers are an old model with no API, so points have to be sent from a small agent installed on each store computer.

risks.description: Unreliable shop internet requires an offline queue that retries sending points. This added about 110 hours that were not in the original estimate on the comparable project.

citations.quote: we had to build an offline queue that retried sending points. That alone was around 110 hours not in the estimate.

risks.description: App store review rejection (for example over account deletion requirements) can delay launch by days, which is dangerous with a fixed anniversary campaign date.

citations.quote: Apple's review rejected the first submission over account deletion, a two-day delay.

risks.description: Marketing-driven deadline tied to the anniversary campaign leaves little room for slippage in the till integration or store rollout.

citations.quote: Marketing owns the project and wants the first version in time for the chain's anniversary campaign.

risks.description: Store staff with little technical training may struggle with the QR scanning workflow and the agent installation, which could affect adoption and support load.

citations.quote: Store staff have almost no technical training.

assumptions: Based mainly on the coffee chain loyalty app (b008), which delivered at 760 hours with nearly identical scope and constraints.
The low end (600) reflects the original estimate for that project, adjusted for fewer stores (22 vs 35), assuming the till agent and offline queue are scoped up front rather than discovered later.
The high end (780) reflects the actual 760 hours plus a small allowance for rollout differences, assuming similar scope including back office and QR scanning.
Assumes cross-platform mobile development, QR code per customer, points, rewards, push notifications and a back office.
Assumes the offline queue (around 110 hours) and the store agent are included from the start.
Excludes importing existing stamp card data and any new till hardware.

citations.quote: Delivered in 760 hours against an estimate of 600.
Back office to create campaigns and see redemptions.

No information on the bakery's till models or store computers, so the agent effort is uncertain.

output.summary: The brief closely matches a past delivered project (b012): an Android rugged-scanner picking app with route guidance, barcode verification, offline mode and a WMS API integration. That project took 690 hours (about $62,000) with 60 pickers. This brief has 40 pickers and appears not to ask for a supervisor screen, so a range around the past actuals with modest adjustments seems reasonable. Device model and Android version, WMS API quality and route logic complexity remain unconfirmed.
open_questions: Which rugged scanner models and Android versions are in use, and can we get devices from week one?
Is the WMS API a documented REST API, and is the API owner available and cooperative?
How is the 'best route' defined: by shelf location sequence from the WMS, or does it need layout-aware path optimisation?
Is a supervisor or productivity screen needed, or is it out of scope?
What offline behaviour is required: how long can scanners be offline, and how should sync conflicts such as stock changes be handled?
Are short-picks, substitutions and quantity confirmation in scope?
Is a pilot in one area planned before full rollout, and what is the target date?
What is the target for wrong orders (currently about 1.5%) and how will it be measured?
Do the scanners use built-in hardware scanning or camera scanning, and which barcode formats are used?

risks.description: Old Android versions on rugged scanners can limit available libraries and add effort. The comparable project lost about 30 hours to this. The brief does not state the device or OS version.

citations.quote: The old Android version limited some libraries and cost about 30 hours.
Scanners run an old Android version.

risks.description: Offline operation in wifi dead zones adds sync and conflict complexity. It worked in the past project because it was planned from the start, so it must be designed in from the beginning and not added later.

citations.quote: Offline mode was planned from the start and worked.
Works offline in dead zones of the warehouse and syncs when connected.

risks.description: Dependence on the WMS API: delays, gaps or an uncooperative API owner would hurt predictability.

citations.quote: a clear process with a cooperative API owner is predictable; test on the real devices from week one.

risks.description: Evidence that the app reduces wrong orders is thin. The past pilot had only four weeks of data, so the benefit case for 1.5% to a lower rate may be hard to prove early.

citations.quote: wrong orders dropped in the pilot aisle, though we only had four weeks of data

risks.description: Late testing on real rugged devices could surface scanner-integration and performance issues, and scan feedback speed drives picker adoption.

citations.quote: Pickers adopted the app quickly because the scan feedback was fast

assumptions: Derived from b012 actual of 690 hours for a near-identical scope (Android rugged scanners, route order, barcode verification, offline sync, WMS REST API).
Low end is lower than the past actual because there are 40 pickers rather than 60 and no supervisor productivity screen is mentioned; assumes it is out of scope.
High end allows for old-Android library workarounds (about 30 hours in the past project), an undocumented WMS API, or route logic more complex than shelf-location ordering.
Assumes a cooperative WMS API owner and access to real devices from week one.
b003 (fleet tracking) is not comparable and was not used.

citations.quote: Delivered in 690 hours against an estimate of 700, on target.
Pick lists downloaded from the warehouse management system, with route order by shelf location.

insufficient_info: Scanner models, Android version and WMS API quality are not specified.
Whether a supervisor screen, reporting or a pilot phase is wanted is not stated.

Is a scoring sheet or credit scoring logic required, or only a checklist?
What management and regulator reports are needed?
Are there existing core banking or loan systems to integrate with, and how are users authenticated (SSO, MFA)?
How many applications per month and how many analysts and approvers?
Are the checklist and approval rules fixed or configurable by the credit union?

output.summary: Educational film publisher wants a web subscription streaming service for about 600 hours of video, with regional licensing limits, rights-holder content protection, payments with trials and coupons, subtitle management, basic analytics, and a fixed festival launch date. One past project (b023, a documentary subscription site) is a very close match and delivered at 1,450 hours against a 1,000-hour estimate. The main drivers of overrun were DRM requirements, library conversion and missing subtitles. The new library is smaller (600 vs 800 hours), so the estimate is adjusted down slightly, but the DRM uncertainty keeps the upper end high. A reduced-catalog launch is a realistic fallback for the festival date.
open_questions: What DRM level and security requirements do the rights holders specify (e.g. Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady, L1 vs L3, watermarking)? Is this confirmed in writing?
Which countries are licensed per title, and is blocking by country enough or are there other restrictions such as time windows?
What is the festival date and what is the minimum catalog and feature set required at launch?
In what formats is the 600 hours stored, and are masters available in good quality?
Do subtitles already exist for all content? In which languages, and in what formats? Who produces missing ones?
Which payment provider and currencies are needed? Is tax/VAT handling required across regions?
Expected subscriber volume and concurrent viewing peaks (affects video platform tier and cost)?
Is there an existing user base or accounts to migrate?
Which analytics are needed (views, churn, per-title reports for rights holders)?
Do the rights holders need royalty or usage reporting?

risks.description: Rights holders may require a specific DRM level that forces a different video platform and player rework, if the video stack is chosen before requirements are confirmed.

citations.quote: Load tests showed the video provider's free tier was not enough, which changed the monthly cost for the client.

Library is about 600 hours vs 800 in b023, so conversion and subtitle effort is reduced somewhat; low end assumes about 20-25% less than b023.

output.summary: The brief asks for a semantic and keyword search tool over a consultancy's archive of proposals and contracts (PDF and Word), with filters, passage highlighting, per-engagement access control, and a requirement that nothing leaves the client's cloud account. One past project (b025, contract search for a law firm) is very close in scope and was delivered in 700 hours for $66,000. The other sources (loan workflow, property portal) are not comparable. The main differences are that archive size, scanned-PDF share and engagement-structure quality are unknown for the new client.
open_questions: How many documents are in the archive, and what is the total volume and date range?
What share are scanned PDFs needing OCR versus born-digital PDFs or Word files?
How are engagements structured today, and is there a reliable mapping from documents to engagements and the people allowed to see them?
Which identity provider and groups should drive access control (e.g. SSO, Azure AD, Okta)?
Which filters are needed (client, year, document type, author, engagement)?
Which cloud provider and which managed services or models are permitted inside the account? Must embedding and language models also run entirely within the account?
Is there a formal search quality target or evaluation requirement, and who will judge relevance?
Do documents need to be split into clauses or sections, or is document-level search with passage highlighting enough?
Are there languages other than English in the documents?
Do access rules change over time (e.g. staff leaving an engagement), and is an audit log of searches or views required?

risks.description: Scanned PDFs require OCR and extraction is messier than expected, adding effort and degrading search quality.

citations.quote: Text extraction from scanned PDFs needed OCR and was messier than expected, around 70 hours more.

citations.quote: The permission model took longer because the matter structure had gaps that the firm had to clean.

risks.description: Access control and document cleaning tend to take more time than the search itself, so estimates focused on search features may run over.

citations.quote: Lesson: access control and document cleaning take more time than the search itself.

citations.quote: Search quality was judged good by the pilot group in informal tests, but we did not run a formal evaluation.

risks.description: The requirement that nothing leaves the cloud account limits the choice of hosted embedding and language model services and may require self-hosted or in-account models, affecting cost and quality.

citations.quote: No document leaves the firm's cloud account.

assumptions: Derived mainly from b025, which delivered in 700 hours against an original estimate of 600; it is the only comparable project.
Range is centered slightly above 700 to allow for unknowns: the new archive size is not given (b025 had about 40,000 documents), and the OCR share and engagement-structure quality are unknown.
Assumes a similar feature set: keyword and semantic search, filters, passage highlighting with link to the original, per-engagement access control, and in-account deployment only.

output.summary: The brief is a one-line request for a modern, good-looking company website with a cost question. It gives no information on company type, site purpose, page count, features (e-commerce, bookings, login, CMS), content readiness, integrations, timeline, or budget. The past projects are all large, feature-heavy builds (listing portal, subscription streaming, store migration, course platform), not comparable to a typical company website, so a cost figure derived from them would be misleading.
open_questions: What does the company do, and what is the main goal of the site (lead generation, brand presence, selling online, recruiting)?
Is this a new site or a redesign/migration of an existing one? If existing, what platform and how much content?
Roughly how many pages or page types are needed?
Are any functional features required: e-commerce, booking, user accounts, multilingual content, blog, search, integrations with CRM or payments?
Who will provide copy, photography, branding and design assets, or is that part of the scope?
Does the client need a CMS so staff can edit content themselves?
What is the budget range and the desired launch date?
What are the 'modern and good looking' references, e.g. example sites the client likes?
Are there SEO, accessibility, or compliance requirements (GDPR, cookie consent)?
Who handles hosting, domain, and ongoing maintenance after launch?

risks.description: Subjective requirements ('modern and good looking') with no references or acceptance criteria invite repeated design revisions and disagreement over what counts as done.
Scope is undefined: without knowing features, page count, or content, cost could range from a small brochure site to a complex platform, risking a mismatched budget expectation.
Content and asset readiness (copy, images, branding) is unknown and commonly delays website projects and inflates cost.
If an existing site is being replaced, migration and preservation of search ranking could add significant work, as seen in a past migration project.

citations.quote: move the shop to a modern platform without losing their search ranking

insufficient_info: The brief does not state the company type, site purpose, features, page count, content readiness, or budget, so no scope can be sized.

The cited past projects (property portal, video subscription site, shoe store migration, course platform) are large custom platform builds with 830 to 1450 hours and are not comparable to a standard company website; using them would produce a misleadingly high or precise figure.
A cost range should wait until the open questions are answered; a short discovery session is recommended.

output.summary: The client needs firmware for a satellite ground-station antenna controller. This includes real-time motor control on a custom microcontroller board, radiation-tolerant design reviews and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing. None of the past projects is comparable: they are web, mobile, SaaS and industrial-data projects with no embedded firmware, motor control, radiation-tolerance or HIL work. I can't give a defensible hours or cost estimate from this evidence, so none is provided. The past projects do give general lessons about hidden integration work and test environments, which I use below as risk signals.
open_questions: Which microcontroller and board? Is the custom board already built and stable, or still in design revision?
What motor types and control loops are needed (stepper, BLDC, servo)? What pointing accuracy, slew rates and tracking loops are required?
What interfaces does the controller need (encoders, limit switches, RS-422, Ethernet, CAN)? Is there a host protocol such as rotctld or a custom one?
What radiation environment applies? Ground-station electronics usually don't face the same radiation as flight hardware, so what does 'radiation-tolerant design review' actually require?
What do the design reviews involve: our participation, formal deliverables, or a specific standard (e.g. ECSS, NASA)?
Does a HIL test rig exist? Who builds and maintains the plant models, and who supplies the hardware?
What are the safety and certification requirements (e.g. end-stops, e-stop, MISRA C, coding standards)?
Who owns the hardware bring-up, board support package and toolchain? Is an RTOS required?
What is the delivery timeline, and how many antennas or sites are involved?
Is there existing firmware or a prototype to build on?

risks.description: Hardware dependency: firmware schedule depends on a custom board that may change or be delayed, and bring-up issues typically surface late. Past projects show that dependence on client-side equipment and environments produced unplanned work.

citations.quote: store computers had different Windows versions and flaky internet, and we had to build an offline queue

risks.description: Unavailable or unreliable test environments can stall integration and testing. HIL rigs, plant models and hardware access are likely to be scarce and need to be confirmed before quoting.

citations.quote: the insurer's test environment was down for weeks

risks.description: Compliance and review requirements may be revealed late. Radiation-tolerance reviews and any applicable standards could add documentation and rework not visible in the brief.

citations.quote: compliance reviews of the prescription flow, which the client only revealed after the first demo

risks.description: External interfaces (encoders, drivers, host control software) may behave differently from their documentation. Sample data and interface specs should be obtained before estimating.

citations.quote: budget extra time for every external API, and ask for sample payloads before the estimate

risks.description: Real-time motor control tuning, timing and safety behaviour require iteration on real hardware and may exceed plans. This is general engineering judgement, not drawn from the past projects.

insufficient_info: No past project involves embedded firmware, real-time motor control, radiation-tolerant design or hardware-in-the-loop testing, so no hours or cost range can be derived from the available actuals.
The brief gives no details on board, motors, interfaces, standards, test rig availability or timeline, so even a rough sizing would be invented precision.
A comparable estimate would need past embedded/aerospace/robotics projects, or a discovery phase to size the work.

sources.text: Delivered in 1,900 hours against an estimate of 1,200, a large overrun. Getting data out of the old controllers took about 500 hours: custom protocol adapters, network approvals and sensors that had to be installed. Without labeled failures we could only build alert rules and simple anomaly detection, not a true failure predictor. The client accepted this after the pilot. Lesson: industrial data projects spend most of the effort on data acquisition, and the machine learning promise must be reduced when there are no labels.
sources.title: Predictive maintenance pipeline

sources.text: Delivered in 1,400 hours against an estimate of 1,100. The three vendor APIs behaved very differently: one had undocumented rate limits, one sent timestamps in local time without a timezone, and one changed its payload format once during the project. Normalizing the data into one model took about 200 hours more than planned. The real-time map was done within the first phase as expected. The fuel report was descoped halfway because one vendor did not expose fuel sensors. The client is happy with the map and the late-delivery alerts. Lesson: budget extra time for every external API, and ask for sample payloads before the estimate.
sources.title: Fleet tracking dashboards

sources.text: A two-person startup wants to launch a personal finance app that connects to users' bank accounts, categorizes spending automatically and gives savings tips. The founders have a design in Figma and some seed money. They contacted us and three other agencies for a quote.
sources.title: Personal finance mobile app

sources.text: Delivered in 760 hours against an estimate of 600. The mobile app was quick. The register agent was the problem: store computers had different Windows versions and flaky internet, and we had to build an offline queue that retried sending points. That alone was around 110 hours not in the estimate. Apple's review rejected the first submission over account deletion, a two-day delay. Lesson: any software installed on the client's old store machines needs its own line in the estimate.
sources.title: Loyalty app for a coffee chain

sources.text: Delivered in 1,100 hours against an estimate of 900. Video itself was easy using a managed video API. The overrun came from the SAML integration (about 90 hours, the insurer's test environment was down for weeks) and from compliance reviews of the prescription flow, which the client only revealed after the first demo. Load tests showed the video provider's free tier was not enough, which changed the monthly cost for the client. Lesson: ask about compliance reviews and test environments before quoting.
sources.title: Telemedicine platform
